name: Fasoracetam

lead: Fasoracetam is a racetam discovered by Nippon Shinyaku in the late 1980s. It was tested for vascular dementia, then repurposed for ADHD and a genetic syndrome, and is now sold online as a nootropic that users take for focus and attention.
It appears to modulate metabotropic glutamate receptors. Human research is limited to small trials. Its role in the nootropic stack is mental performance.

paras: It is taken as a nootropic supplement, typically in racetam-style stacks for study and work.
It is not approved for any use. Side-effect information is limited to small trials.

angle.text: Fasoracetam is a racetam that nootropic users take for focus and attention, following its trials in ADHD. It sits in the nootropic stack for better mental performance.

lead: Fasoracetam is an experimental racetam-class drug discovered by Nippon Shinyaku in the late 1980s and never marketed. It was tested for vascular dementia, then repurposed for ADHD and later other conditions [1]. It appears to modulate metabotropic glutamate receptors [1].

It is sold online as a nootropic, and people who take nootropics describe the aim as sharper focus and mental stamina rather than a change in physical looks. Fasoracetam is not directly connected to physical appearance; its place in a looks-focused wiki is as one of the cognitive supplements that appear in self-improvement stacks, where users hope for better concentration for study, training or work [1][2].

The research that exists is clinical and aimed at medical conditions: phase 3 trials in vascular dementia, a 2018 study in adolescents with ADHD who carry variants in glutamate-receptor genes, and a 2022 phase 2 trial in 22q11 deletion syndrome [1][3][4]. The drug is not approved for any indication in the United States and is a prescription-only substance (Schedule 4) in Australia [1].

paras: Fasoracetam is a derivative of pyroglutamic acid with a piperidine amide, classed with the racetams. Wikipedia describes it as appearing to modulate and stimulate all three groups of metabotropic glutamate receptors, with rodent studies reporting improvements in some aspects of cognition [1]. Unlike many racetams it is not described as acting mainly on ionotropic AMPA receptors; preclinical work points to group II mGluR effects on adenylyl cyclase signalling, with additional effects on GABA-B receptor expression and acetylcholine release reported in animals [5].

It is orally bioavailable, with 79 to 97 percent bioavailability reported in animals and an elimination half-life of roughly 4 to 6.5 hours; it is excreted mostly unchanged in urine [1][5]. In adolescents, peak plasma concentrations occurred about 1.3 to 1.9 hours after dosing, with exposure increasing in proportion across the tested range [3][5].

Scientists at the Japanese company Nippon Shinyaku developed fasoracetam in the late 1980s, under the codes NS-105 and LAM-105, and took it through phase 3 trials in vascular dementia before abandoning that indication for lack of sufficient efficacy [1][6]. The compound was later repurposed. Hakon Hakonarson's group at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia studied it for ADHD; his company neuroFix acquired Nippon Shinyaku's clinical data, Medgenics acquired neuroFix in 2015, and Medgenics renamed itself Aevi Genomic Medicine on 16 December 2016 [1]. Trials in adolescents with ADHD and mGluR gene mutations began in 2016 and were reported in Nature Communications in January 2018 [1][3]. By 2018 development under Avalo Therapeutics (formerly Cerecor) had been discontinued, and in October 2023 Nobias Therapeutics was running a phase 2 trial of NB-001 in 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome [1][4].

Chemically fasoracetam is (5R)-5-(piperidine-1-carbonyl)pyrrolidin-2-one [1]. A 2017 study of its solid-state forms found two hydrated and one anhydrous crystal form, with the monohydrate stable under ambient conditions and melting at about 57 degrees Celsius, a low value that the authors said could complicate formulation [7].

Nippon Shinyaku's phase 3 trials in vascular dementia did not show sufficient efficacy [1]. A 2018 five-week, open-label, single-blind, placebo-controlled study in 30 adolescents aged 12 to 17 with ADHD who carry mutations in mGluR network genes reported safety, pharmacokinetic and response data; mutation status was double-blinded [3]. Wikipedia characterizes the broader ADHD results as not statistically significant and any benefit as possibly limited to people with specific mGluR variants, estimated at around 10 percent of ADHD cases [1].

A 2019 systematic review of randomised trials of novel non-stimulant ADHD compounds covered the drug among its pipeline [2]. A phase 2 trial in children and adolescents with 22q11 deletion syndrome started in February 2022 and was completed with 37 participants [4]. Patent literature also lists fasoracetam among racetam compounds proposed for apathy syndrome [8]. No study has examined fasoracetam in healthy people seeking cognitive or appearance benefits.

Fasoracetam is sold online by supplement vendors as a nootropic and is described as used outside medical supervision [1]. It is Schedule 4 (prescription only) in Australia under the Poisons Standard since February 2020 and is not FDA-approved in the United States [1].

timeline.event: Nippon Shinyaku develops fasoracetam for vascular dementia [1].
A Drugs in R&D entry catalogues the compound under the codes LAM 105 and NS 105 [6].
Medgenics acquires neuroFix, which holds fasoracetam clinical data [1].
Medgenics renames itself Aevi Genomic Medicine; ADHD trials in adolescents with mGluR variants begin [1].
Nature Communications reports fasoracetam in adolescents with ADHD and glutamatergic gene variants [3].
A phase 2 trial in 22q11 deletion syndrome starts [4].
